Full marks for considering those with colour blindness, and acting with compassion. It doesn’t look good, mind. It’s just not Arsenal.After a moment to remember the victims of the devastating floods in Nepal, Arsenal get the ball rolling. A blistering atmosphere at the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona; did anyone expect anything else? Continue reading...
bodyEn: 90 min +2: Now Neres whacks the ball away in frustration, but he’s not booked, the referee having missed it. Gabriel is furious, and runs the risk of picking up a card himself by telling it as he sees it.
90 min +1: Odegaard is booked for lashing a dead ball away, with Napoli preparing to take a quick free kick deep in their own territory.
90 min: There will be four additional minutes.

89 min: Neres pings a cute pass down the inside-left channel, and suddenly De Bruyne is free, on the corner of the six-yard box. De Bruyne has only Raya to beat, but rolls a ball across the face of goal, hoping to find Lucca instead. Lucca’s not there. The crowd groan again, at the latest of De Bruyne’s egregious errors. It’s not been a banner evening for one of the genuine greats of the last decade.
88 min: … Napoli counter, but Neres can’t get on the end of a pass down the middle. Arsenal were light at the back.
87 min: A corner for Arsenal on the right. Madueke wanders in and aims for the top left. The shot is deflected wide left for another corner, from which …
86 min: Lucca is booked for knocking into Gabriel.

85 min: Gilmour is robbed by Zubimendi and sends Guimarães away on the counter. Guimarães slips in Madueke to his right. Madueke is clear! But he can’t slip the ball under Milinković-Savić, who blocks, then spins up and stops Madueke rolling into the empty net. Madueke instead cuts back for Tzolis, whose drive hits the nearest defender. Not sure how Napoli kept that out, but they collectively managed it.
84 min: Favasuli tries to take on Hincapie in a footrace down the right, but the defender’s letting nobody past.
82 min: Guimarães looks for the top-left corner from 25 yards. High and wide. Before Milinković-Savić restarts the game, Zubimendi comes on for White.

80 min: Lucca barrels after a long punt down the middle, but can’t get the ball under control. On the touchline, Massimiliano Allegri, staring down the barrel of a third consecutive defeat so early in his reign, rants and raves in the classic continental style.
78 min: That’s now four assists in five games for Tzolis. Arsenal fans are in great voice, the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona otherwise quiet.
77 min: Napoli respond with a double change, replacing Hojlund and Lobotka with Neres and Lucca.

Arsenal get patient … and get their reward. Some metronomic passing, then suddenly a shift through the gears, as White and Tzolis combine crisply down the inside-right, cutting back for Odegaard, who pearls a rising shot across Milinković-Savić, off the left-hand post and in! What a strike!
73 min: Gyökeres and Saka, who have both been ineffective this evening, make way for Madueke and Havertz.
72 min: This game has become scrappy, and it’s probably doing Napoli more of a favour.

70 min: Tzolis meets a ball dropping towards the Napoli penalty spot … and nearly launches his shot into orbit. In terms of slapstick and comedic timing, it was almost perfect. In footballing terms, not so much.
68 min: The pace drops. It is warm in Naples after all, 27 degrees centigrade at kick-off according to Uefa’s official thermometer.
66 min: A double change for Arsenal as Merino and Eze make way for Guimarães and Tzolis.

65 min: De Bruyne, under no pressure, butchers a simple pass meant for Lobotka, in acres on the right flank. The crowd groan as the ball sails into the stand. The veteran midfielder has had a bit of a shocker so far.
63 min: Rice makes himself a little bit of time and space to the right of the Napoli D, then lashes a wild shot high and well wide right.

62 min: Hojlund strides down the left but can’t get past Gabriel as he reaches the edge of the box. His shot is deflected, and De Bryune chases after the loose ball, but he doesn’t have the legs to get past Hincapie.
61 min: Vergara also wastes little time in getting involved … but upon tearing down the left, he ruins it all by yanking a dismal cross straight into the arms of Raya.

60 min: The newly arrived Favasuli comes sliding in on Merino at 101 miles per hour. He times his tackle perfectly – just – and the crowd enjoyed that very much. A nanosecond one way or the other, though, and the Napoli sub would have been in a world of bother. He was fully committed, put it that way.

58 min: Santos left White in the dust there, such a cheeky and skilful run, but looks to have injured himself in the process. He departs, along with Politano, the pair replaced by Favasuli and Vergara.

56 min: Santos knocks the ball past White down the left and rounds the defender, then tears away. Lovely play. He shuttles the ball infield for De Bruyne, who looks for Hojlund but his radar is wonky. That’s not his first misplaced pass of the evening, and the home crowd aren’t 100 percent happy with him.
55 min: Rice clumsily clanks into Santos, and pressure that had been building for several minutes is suddenly released. Napoli so grateful for the breather.
53 min: Arsenal are pushing Napoli back. The hosts can’t get out. There’s no option for them other than long to Hojlund. The nearly-all-reds well on top.
52 min: Odegaard, dictating the tempo now from a deep position, loops another pass into the Napoli box. Again for White, but this time down the left, and not so elegant as before. Goal kick.

50 min: Odegaard suddenly springs into action, elegantly wedging a pass down the inside-right channel and into the box for White, who heads across the face of goal. Hincapie should ram home from close range, but somehow manages to leather the ball over the bar. Not for the first time tonight we say: Arsenal should be leading.
49 min: To a chorus of impatient whistling, Arsenal stroke the ball around, this way and that, 30 yards from the Napoli goal. There’s no way through the defence.

47 min: Milinković-Savić has got the mother of all hipster’s beards. He looks like he should be behind the counter at a record store, or running a micro-brewery. While he finds his feet at one end of the park, Napoli make good down the other, and Gilmour takes a whack from distance. Easy for Raya.

Napoli get the second half started. Milinković-Savić has replaced Meret in their goal. “As Big Ron used to say, ‘If you look good, you play good’,” begins Alan Baverstock. “Well, Arsenal are looking crap in all red with white sleeves once again, as anyone would, so don’t expect too much. So close, yet so far from Bill Shankly’s switch to all red at Liverpool: ‘The players looked like giants,’ he said, ‘And we played like giants.’”
Half-time fag break postbag ... which for some reason is tobacco-infused.

“Well, sir, can they boogie without the Great Scott? Presumably Mr McT is in the stand somewhere, a crafty fag on the go, cupped between thumb and index finger and held behind the back, just in case the cameras spot him” – Justin Kavanagh
“Just checking: Gyökeres is still there, right? He hasn’t gone for a lie down or some mid-half snus?” – Adam Walker

“I understand that winning games builds psychological momentum, but I feel that Arteta could use some of these essentially meaningless league phase matches to give his most overworked players the night off. Does Rice need to be on the field? Yeah, if you want to maximise your chances of winning this game. But given how exhausted he looked at the end of last season, it might be good to rest him” – Kári Tulinius

“Can you put that photo of Kai Havertz back up? At least then Arsenal fans will have a useful striker to look at. And it’d be no more immoble than the one on the pitch” – Charles Anaki [Click here to relive some of that Hot Havertz Action]
Half-time ad break. Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!
It’s been good, but not great.

45 min +2: Saka goes long. There’s a bit of pinball, before Hincapie tries to catch Meret out with a cheeky threaded shot towards the bottom left. There’s no pace on the shot, and it’s easy for the keeper.
45 min +1: The first of two additional minutes, and Konsa’s sheer determination down the right wins Arsenal a corner. Just enough time to take it!

45 min: Arsenal should be leading. Odegaard slides a pass down the inside-right channel to release Saka into the Napoli box. Saka is one on one with Meret, and looks for the top left, but gets it all wrong, the ball sailing miles off target to the left. The offside flag pops up to momentarily save Saka’s blushes … but replays show he was comfortably onside. That’s a huge opportunity passed up.

43 min: The free kick, then. A big faff, and a big waste. But Arsenal come again, Odegaard curling in from the left. Meret, who looks fit and healthy to the naked and untrained eye, punches clear acrobatically.

42 min: This game has slipped into Basketball Mode. Saka with a dribble down the right. His cutback for Rice is intercepted. Olivera probes down the left but can’t get past Konsa. Eze scampers up the other end, and is skittled by Gilmour, who goes into the book. A free kick 30 yards out, just to the left of centre.

40 min: Olivera swats Saka off the ball and sends Santos off on a wild run down the left. Santos nearly gets the better of Konsa … but the Arsenal defender somehow sticks to his side like glue, and eventually does some swatting of his own. Santos goes over, and wants a free kick, but he’s not getting one.
39 min: Politano’s in-swinging shot from the right flies straight at Raya. Arsenal counter, and Saka hoicks a dreadful effort miles over the bar.
38 min: … though having said that, Napoli’s back-up keeper Milinković-Savić is furiously prepping in the dugout. Meret puts his boot through a clearance, meanwhile, so perhaps all’s well. Let’s see.
37 min: Meret is fine to continue, and restarts the game. Everyone refreshed.
36 min: The game doesn’t restart immediately, because Meret has a problem. On come the physio. Everyone else takes the opportunity to snorkel some isotonic treats.
35 min: Rice buys a ticket from 25 yards. High and wide.

bodyEn: Raphinha let his goals do the talking after being omitted from the Ballon d’Or shortlist, striking twice as Barcelona eased to a 5-1 win over Feyenoord in the Champions League.

The Brazilian was a surprise omission from this week’s 30-strong list of candidates for the prestigious award but brushed any disappointment aside to continue his early season hot streak at a rain-soaked Camp Nou. The forward finished brilliantly in the third minute and added a second just before the hour mark to down the Eredivisie side and take his tally to eight goals in six outings at the start of the campaign.

The summer signing Karim Adeyemi produced a stunning finish, Lamine Yamal stroked a free-kick through a gap in the Dutch wall and recent arrival Gabriel Jesus opened his account for the club just two minutes after stepping off the bench.
There was little to celebrate for Giovanni van Bronckhorst on his Barça return but Sem Steijn gave the visiting fans something to enjoy when he poked in at far post late on.
Elsewhere, Stuttgart’s Ermedin Demirovic struck a 12-minute first-half hat-trick to ⁠earn ⁠a ​3-1 victory over Viking Stavanger.

He opened the ​scoring after 20 minutes with a touch at the near post, but Viking, making their first appearance in the league phase of the Champions League, were level two minutes later when Zlatko Tripic finished a ⁠swift counter-attack with his left foot. Demirovic quickly re-established the lead ​in the ​26th minute and then completed ​the hat-trick with a hooked volley six minutes later.

items.titleEn: Team news: Four switches for Napoli test
items.summaryEn: Find out the side that Mikel Arteta has selected for our first Champions League game of the season at the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona
bodyEn: Mikel Arteta has made four changes to his side that will kick off our Champions League campaign at Napoli tonight, with Viktor Gyokeres, Ebere Eze, Piero Hincapie and Mikel Merino getting their first starts of the season.

The quartet come into our line-up following our 2-1 success against Chelsea on Sunday, with the Swedish striker getting the nod over Kai Havertz, who will hope to continue his excellent scoring start to 2026/27 from the bench.

Hincapie starts at left-back with Riccardo Calafiori dropping down to the replacements back in his homeland, while Merino is preferred to Myles Lewis-Skelly in midfield. Meanwhile, Eze comes in for Christos Tzolis, as the boss opts to rotate his side that has won all four games so far this term.

As for our opponents, Massimiliano Allegri made three alterations to his side, which allowed a two-goal lead to slip in a 3-2 defeat at Inter Milan on Saturday - their second successive defeat in Serie A.
Frank Anguissa picked up a groin injury in that game and is replaced in midfield by Kevin De Bruyne, while fellow Premier League alum Billy Gilmour is also included, with Antonio Vergara demoted.
There is also a change at left-back, with Leonardo Spinazzola dropped and Mathias Olivera taking his spot.
LINE-UPS

Arsenal: Raya, White, Konsa, Gabriel, Hincapie, Merino, Rice, Odegaard, Saka, Eze, Gyokeres.Subs: Arrizabalaga, Meslier, Calafiori, Salmon, Lewis-Skelly, Zubimendi, Guimaraes, Tzolis, Madueke, Dowman, Havertz.

Napoli: Meret, Di Lorenzo, Marin, Rrahmani, Olivera, Lobotka, Gilmour, De Bruyne, Politano, Santos, Hojlund.Subs: Milinkovic-Savic, Contini, Favasuli, Spinazzola, Badiashile, Beukema, Vergara, Neres, Lucca.

items.titleEn: Horseman hails 'world class' winner from Munoz
items.summaryEn: David Horseman on our 2-1 win over Napoli and Munoz's incredible winning goal
bodyEn: David Horseman described Luis Munoz's winner against Napoli as world class, as we picked up a 2-1 victory in our UEFA Youth League opener.

Munoz, aged 14 years and 263 days old, became the second-youngest scorer in Youth League history, just three days older than record holder Max Dowman, when he pinged his effort into the top corner in stoppage time.
After the match, a delighted Horseman reflected on the incredible effort: "The finish is just world class.

"On any stage, that's a goal that's fit to win any game. But we know that we're not just giving people token games. We brought a squad that we thought could win the game, and he was part of it. He come on and had the decisive moment.
"But it is a world class goal, and I don't use that word lightly; that's for sure."
Andre Harriman-Annous pounced to give us the lead on a scorching hot day in Naples, pressing well to force the error from the Napoli backline, delighting our head coach.

"While the angles weren't always quite right, we always had intent with our press and they did persist with it. Even when you can see they've got nothing left in their legs, they're still trying to do it. They're a really good group of kids who want to learn."
There were plenty of chances in the match, with Napoli having 28 shots to our 14. That meant goalkeeper Jack Porter had a busy afternoon at the Giuseppe Piccolo.
Assessing the win, David said: "It was a very tough game and a game where, if we're honest, we rode our luck at times. Jack made some brilliant saves.
"We had a few good spells in the game, but not as much as we would like. We didn't feel in control enough. But we have really good players we forced the mistake through the high press.
"Then one moment of magic from another ridiculously young player, which won the game. I've only been here a year, but over the last five years, we've had 50 of those games and lost.
"This competition is about trying to win and develop within the winning part of it. We've made a good start. We've got a really tough run of games, so we needed to get off to a quick start.
"This sets us up for the Lille game after the international break to hopefully really have a go at getting through the group stage this year."

items.titleEn: U19s report: Napoli 1-2 Arsenal
items.summaryEn: All the details from our opening UEFA Youth League match of the season
bodyEn: Luis Munoz's stunning late strike helped us kick off our UEFA Youth League campaign with a 2-1 victory over Napoli at the Stadio Giuseppe Piccolo.
Andre Harriman-Annous tapped home after a loose pass in defence from the hosts in an action-packed first half.

We hit the bar twice through Axel Donczew and Maalik Hashi before Milton Pereyra levelled for the hosts on 58 minutes. The game looked to be ending all square before Munoz's incredible effort found the top corner from the edge of the box to secure all three points.
PORTER TO THE RESCUE
The first chance fell to Francesco De Stefano, who drove at the heart of our defence before unleashing a low drive that was well saved by Jack Porter.

The goalkeeper had to be alert once again moments later as Mohamed Mane raced through. His effort was well saved before the ball rebounded off the striker towards goal, only to be cleared off the line by Josh Ogunnaike.
Porter then made up for his own misplaced pass out from the back, which found Mane inside the box. The striker could not get past our goalkeeper, who tipped his shot wide.

We had our first chance after 17 minutes. Ogunnaike's dangerous cross from a free-kick found Brayden Clarke. The defender's header fell into the path of Emerson Nwaneri, who could only fire straight at Claudio Pugliese from close range.
HARD WORK PAYS OFF

We were growing into the game. Centre-back Elijah Upson, on UEFA Youth League debut for us, was able to drive through the Napoli midfield with ease to help create space for the front line. Maalik Hashi was able to find a pocket of space on the edge of the box to get his shot away, which went just wide of Pugliese's far post.

Our hard work paid off in the 28th minute. Good pressure from Ife Ibrahim on the goalkeeper and then Agostino Branchizio forced the defender to pass straight across his box and into the path of Harriman-Annous to tap home.
Napoli responded almost immediately through captain Pereyra, who looked certain to tap home but found Porter in the way to deny him from point-blank range.

The hosts were looking sharper after the hydration break in the Naples sun. A fine through-ball from Francisco Barido found Mykyta Melnyk, who tried to wrong-foot Porter with his shot, only to hit the post.

Porter produced his latest superb save just before half-time. A long cross found Melnyk at the back post, who set the ball back to captain Pereyra for a first-time finish that was pawed away by our goalkeeper.

There was just time for one last effort in the half for us as we rattled the crossbar after good work down the right-hand side, allowing Donczew to fire his effort off the woodwork. The rebound then fell kindly into the hands of Pugliese before referee Ante Culina blew his whistle for half-time.
NAPOLI BREAKTHROUGH

David Horseman made two subs at half-time, introducing Igor Tyjon and Saurap Sampang. Tyjon's good work helped launch a swift counter-attack, allowing Nwaneri got a shot away, but Pugliese saved well low to his right.
Sampang was immediately tested at right-back, as Napoli wing-back Christian Liccardo got beyond the youngster to square to Pereyra, who struck hard but Porter was a match to it.

Tyjon was causing all sorts of issues to the Napoli backline. The attacker, who signed for us this summer from Blackburn Rovers, jinked his way into the box and squared to the onrushing Hashi, who dug out an effort which flicked the crossbar on its way over.

Napoli had 20 shots in the first half, and they made the breakthrough 13 minutes into the second period. Liccardo was able to get away from Sampang and square for Melnyk at the back post. His effort was well blocked by Ogunnaike and fell to Theo Julienne, whose loose touch saw the ball fall to Pereyra, who fired home first time to level the match.
MAGNIFICENT MUNOZ
Our team took on an even younger look to it for the final 13 minutes, as Luis Munoz and Elyon Mbala were introduced by Horseman.
The hosts thought they had a winner with six minutes to play as Alessandro Rovetini lobbed Porter, but forward Ella Favicchio was given offside for his role in the build-up.
Substitute Rovetini was almost in again, meeting Porter on the edge of his box, but the goalkeeper just managed to block the effort as the hosts sensed a victory.
Both sides weren't content with a point and searched for a winner in six minutes of stoppage time. Munoz's dangerous cross evaded everyone as we couldn't tap home.

But we found our winner deep into stoppage time with a beauty from Munoz. Tyjon did well to win the ball back and fire out to Munoz, who became the youngest player in Youth League history last season, lashed his effort into the top corner from the angle.
Napoli almost levelled in the dying moments, but sub Chiaiese headed onto the post and wide as we picked up a huge victory on the road.
WHAT IT MEANS
Following our win in Naples, we'll be looking to continue our form and secure a top 22 finish in order to reach the knockout stages of the competition for the first time in this format.
WHAT NEXT
Our next UEFA Youth League match will be next month, when we take on French side Lille on Tuesday, October 13, at 1pm.
As for our other age groups, our under-18s are back in action on Saturday, September 12 against Crystal Palace. Our under-21s face Chelsea on the same day in Premier League 2.
LINE-UPS
Napoli: Pugliese, Branchizio, Lieto, Zappala, Liccardo (Chiaiese 83') , Chiummariello, De Stefano (Favicchio 80') , Melnyk, Barido (Riccio 55'), Milton Pereyra (Rovetini 83'), Mane (Esposito 46')
Subs not used: Spinelli, Lepre, Picardi, Chiaiese, D'Angelo, Rovetini
Arsenal: Porter, Ogunnaike, Clarke, Upson, Hamill (Sampang 46'), Julienne (Mbala 77'), Ibrahim (Murisa 67'), Hashi (Munoz 77'), Nwaneri, Harriman-Annous, Donczew (Tyjon 46')
Subs not used: Talbot, O'Neill, Maghoma, Abubakar

items.titleEn: Riccardo Calafiori named men's Player of the Month
items.summaryEn: Our full-back has made a flying start to the season with a goal and two assists
bodyEn: Riccardo Calafiori has been named our men's Player of the Month for August after a fantastic start to the 2026/27 season.
The Italian provided a goal contribution in each of our first three games of the campaign with a goal and two assists, as well as helping us to keep clean sheets in all three matches.
It was a lightning quick start to the new season for Riccardo, as he scored just 23 seconds into the Community Shield against Manchester City, which we went on to win 3-0 in Cardiff.

We followed that up with another 3-0 win in our Premier League opener against Championship champions Coventry City, and this time our no.33 provided the assist for the opening goal, setting up Kai Havertz to score the first goal of the new season.

Ten days later, we rounded off our perfect month with another three points and another clean sheet with a 1-0 win over Aston Villa, and once again our Italian was involved in the crucial moment, setting up Bukayo Saka to score the winner.
Riccardo won August's award with a dominant 74% of the vote, winning out over Martin Odegaard, Bukayo Saka and Gabriel.

items.titleEn: Revitalised Ødegaard’s forward thinking gives Arsenal new lines of attack
items.summaryEn: Midfielder has been pivotal to the champions’ rampant start, becoming a potent threat with his runs into the boxAs Christos Tzolis cut in from the left flank and drove towards the penalty area, Kai Havertz could see history repeating itself.Tzolis had done just the same on his competitive debut for Arsenal against Manchester City in the Community Shield a few weeks earlier, running at his opposition full-back, cutting inside and driving at goal, before fizzing a ball towards the penalty spot. Continue reading...
bodyEn: As Christos Tzolis cut in from the left flank and drove towards the penalty area, Kai Havertz could see history repeating itself.

Tzolis had done just the same on his competitive debut for Arsenal against Manchester City in the Community Shield a few weeks earlier, running at his opposition full-back, cutting inside and driving at goal, before fizzing a ball towards the penalty spot.

Martin Ødegaard was the grateful recipient, arriving just behind Havertz to take the ball smoothly into his path. He then faked a shot to send Gianluigi Donnarumma the wrong way before passing into the empty net.
With the scores level early in the second half of Arsenal’s win against Chelsea on Sunday, Tzolis did something very similar.

This time, his pass was intended for Havertz, but it was played ever so slightly behind the German. But Havertz had watched this before. He knew that Ødegaard, upon seeing Tzolis cut in, would have tiptoed into the penalty area.

Havertz produced a moment of genius to turn Tzolis’s slightly misplaced pass into a perfect assist, lifting his foot over the ball to leave it for his captain. Ødegaard again took the ball under his control with one touch, before this time lifting it over Emiliano Martínez to put Arsenal into a lead they would not surrender.
Ødegaard getting into more advanced positions has been an early theme of this season. He has three goals in four appearances, after scoring once in 36 outings last season.

There has clearly been an effort from Mikel Arteta and his staff to get their fit-again midfielder into attacking areas more consistently. In Premier League games this season, Ødegaard is making 3.2 high-intensity runs per 90 minutes into the opposition’s box while Arsenal have possession, up from 1.4 per 90 last term.
It’s only a small sample size from this season, but the fact that his numbers have more than doubled makes it significant nonetheless. And most important, his goal threat has clearly skyrocketed.

Similarly, he has made seven off-ball runs to make himself a cross option for a teammate in three Premier League games, almost matching his tally from last season (10). On a per-90 basis, that’s 0.65 to 2.8, or more than a fourfold increase. One of those runs led to his goal in the season opener against Coventry.

After an injury-disrupted couple of years, it appears the far-from-linear rise of the 27-year-old has taken a steep, upward turn for the better. And, for an Arsenal team looking imperious this season, that is a very positive sign.

Their captain played his part in their 2025-26 title triumph, but he probably feels more driven than most at the club to repeat the trick. He missed a big chunk of the season with a series of recurring knee injuries, and when he was available he was used sparingly.

He played 1,371 of a possible 3,420 minutes in the league – a scratch over 40.0% – and although he was available for the run-in, playing in key games and in Arsenal’s run to the Champions League final, he was a long way from the key man he has been since his permanent move to the club in the summer of 2021.

Back then Arsenal were signing a hugely talented No 10, but Ødegaard has developed into more of a No 8, a rounded midfielder who drops deep to get on the ball in front of the opposition’s midfield and moves it around the pitch.

The evidence this season suggests that we should expect to see him getting closer to Havertz more often (while also continuing to do the job of a No 8). Havertz isn’t the most reliable goalscorer, but he is an excellent and intelligent centre-forward who performs more of a false 9 role, and he needs more runners ahead of him than Viktor Gyökeres.

It appears this season that Arteta is going to prefer using Havertz up front, which will increase the need for Ødegaard to score more consistently. After the Norwegian’s start, he should at the very least challenge his season-best 15 goals in all competitions from 2022-23. He is averaging 5.6 high-intensity runs ahead of the ball per 90 this season, up from 3.9 last term.

He seems to have benefited from this summer’s World Cup, where he played a key role in his team’s run to the quarter-finals. Only Michael Olise (seven) got more assists at the tournament than Ødegaard (four).

There is pressure on him at club level, though. Eberechi Eze is breathing down his neck after standing in for him for large swathes of last season, though Arteta clearly prefers Ødegaard in the middle, perhaps for his defensive work, positioning and ability to coach Arsenal’s press on the pitch.
But there is just as much pressure on him to stay fit. He started 32, 37 and 35 of a possible 38 Premier League games in his first three full seasons, but has managed 26 then 16 in the past two.
He needs to prove he can stay fit, because not only are Arsenal better with him, but he is more likely to maintain his best form that way.

Ødegaard is showing his best in the early part of 2026-27. He is, along with Chelsea’s Morgan Rogers, one of only two players with at least 1.0 expected goals and 1.0 expected assists in the Premier League, highlighting his all-round attacking game.

Only seven players have played a role in more open-play shot-ending sequences than him (20), and he leads the Premier League for the number of such sequences where he took the shot and was involved in the buildup (four).

It helps that Arsenal look a very functional team, and have benefited from limited changes in personnel over the summer. But how much is that functionality a cause of Ødegaard’s form and how much is it a result? During his time at the club Arsenal have mounted sustained challenges for the Premier League title, and that is surely no coincidence.
Ødegaard is looking back to his best and then some, and that is ominous news for the rest of the Premier League.

items.titleEn: Preview: Napoli v Arsenal
items.summaryEn: Get team news, stats, TV coverage, tactics and more ahead of our opening Champions League game of 2026/27 against Napoli at the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona
bodyEn: The familiar sound of the Champions League theme music will dance back into our lives on Wednesday, as we kick-start our quest to go one step further than last season and get our hands on Europe’s top trophy with a trip to Napoli (8pm UK).

After our heartbreaking penalty shootout loss to Paris Saint-Germain last May, the first step towards landing the big prize starts at the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona in southern Italy, as we aim to extend our incredible 12-game winning run in group-stage matches in the competition, stretching back to November 2024.

Given the huge tests that have been thrown our way in Europe in recent times, we have only lost one of our last 12 away games in the Champions League, which bodes well for the challenge of Gli Azzurri and their passionate supporters as we aim to continue our perfect start to 2026/27 by returning to these shores with a fifth successive victory.
ALLEGRI’S SLOW START

After finishing second in Serie A last term, Napoli entered this campaign under new management as six-time Scudetto winner Massimiliano Allegri took the reins from Antonio Conte and won his first match in charge, kicking off the league campaign with a 2-0 win at Genoa.

However, their only home game this term saw them beaten 2-1 by Como, followed by a 2-0 lead against reigning champions Inter Milan at the San Siro, but they succumbed to a 3-2 defeat after conceding the winner in the 91st minute.

A summer of limited transfer activity saw them capture previous loanees Vanja Milinkovic-Savic, Alisson Santos and last season’s top scorer Rasmus Hojlund on permanent deals, while Benoît Badiashile arrived from Chelsea on loan. Allegri will be tasked with improving European displays after a disappointing 30th-place finish and instant elimination in last season’s competition.
WHAT THE MANAGERS SAY

Arteta: “We know what this competition means to all of us, the experience of last year as well, so we need to start with the first game in a really, really tough place, but really excited to start the campaign.

“It will be a really tough place, I've been in that stadium before, I know the atmosphere they create, their record at home is really, really strong. They have a very experienced manager, a lot of players that played in the league as well, so we know the challenge ahead. We are prepared and we're ready to go.”

Allegri: "Every game starts at 0-0, but clearly Arsenal are favourites. We'll need to show our strength and ability to be competitive. We'll approach the game with determination and pride as we try to get a positive result.
"We have to turn over a new leaf. We face a different challenge tomorrow. We'll need to put in a technically excellent performance and be able to defend better than we did against Como and Inter."
TEAM NEWS
Jurrien Timber’s recovery from his groin injury has now seen him join in with first-team training, and he has travelled with the squad to Naples.

Cristhian Mosquera missed our win against Chelsea on Sunday after picking up a slight issue against Aston Villa but isn’t yet ready to return, while William Saliba is our one long-term absentee with his back injury.

As for our opponents, Scott McTominay underwent minor heart surgery earlier this week and will be out until October, while Italian international centre-back Alessandro Buongiorno underwent knee surgery in the summer and remains out, while Andre-Frank Zambo Anguissa will be missing with a groin injury.
Brazilian strikers Giovane and David Neres are dealing with hernia and knee problems respectively, while young Luca Marianucci suffered a knee injury in pre-season.
TALKING TACTICS

Adrian Clarke: Allegri is known for building pragmatic, defensively solid sides, so we can expect our opponents to focus on keeping their shape. They have lined up in a 4-3-3 in all three Serie A games so far with two direct wingers, Matteo Politano and Alisson Santos flanking centre forward Hojlund.

While they have good technicians who can look after the ball, the early games have pointed to a more counter-attacking style. Averaging just 44.5% possession, they are unlikely to seek total control in this contest. Napoli are not an aggressive pressing side, but they will look to create turnovers from a mid-block base before using the pace and power of their front three. Hojlund wants to run the channels, while Brazilian left winger Alisson Santos is a terrific ball carrier who likes to cut inside and shoot.

Central midfield is usually an area of strength, but with McTominay and Anguissa unavailable, the door may open for Kevin De Bruyne to make his first start of the campaign. In three substitute outings, the Belgian has created seven chances, so he has perhaps earned a place in the starting XI.

Allegri's defensive resilience is currently a work in progress, so this could be a good time to play them. Napoli conceded twice from set pieces against Inter Milan on the weekend, so they may feel uncomfortable when we have corners and free kicks. The stats tell us they have not been as compact as their wily head coach would prefer, as they have faced 61 shots in their three outings, the second most in Italy’s top-flight.
FACTS AND STATS

We have only lost one of our previous seven games against Italian opponents anywhere (W5 D1), but triumphed in one of our last six games on Italian soil in the Champions League - in January in a 3-1 win at Inter Milan.

Napoli have lost just two of their last 21 home Champions League games (W12 D7), but one of those was their last one, against Chelsea in January. In 37 Champions League/European Cup home matches, they have never suffered successive defeats.

We were the only team who didn’t lose a single game in normal time in the 2025/26 Champions League (W11 D4 L0), and only trailed for 42 minutes and 48 seconds, the fewest of any team. Despite playing 15 games, we also conceded the fewest goals of any team in the 2025/26 season (7).
Kai Havertz has scored seven goals across his last 10 Champions League games, just one fewer than in his 53 previous appearances in the competition.
David Raya has kept a clean sheet in 53% of his starts in the Champions League (19/36), the highest percentage of any goalkeeper in the competition (min. 25 starts).
Kevin De Bruyne has been directly involved in 12 goals in his last 17 starts against us across all competitions (8 goals, 4 assists), including five in his most recent three (3 goals, 2 assists).
Since 2024/25, Gabriel has won 82 of his 121 duels in the Champions League. Of the 174 players to contest 100+ duels in the competition in this period, his success rate is the highest (68%).
MATCH OFFICIALS

Swedish official Glenn Nyberg will take charge of this fixture, our first reunion with him since the 2023/24 campaign where he oversaw our 2-1 win at Sevilla, as well as our quarter-final first leg against Bayern Munich when we drew 2-2 at Emirates Stadium, when he awarded the visitors a penalty.

A top-flight official in his homeland since 2013, Nyberg was added to FIFA’s list three years later and has refereed games at Euro 2024 and last summer's World Cup. In 17 Champions League games over the past four seasons, he has sent off only one player and awarded six penalties.
Referee: Glenn Nyberg (SWE)Assistants: Mahbod Beigi, Andreas Soderkvist (SWE)Fourth official: Adam Ladeback (SWE)VAR: Carlos del Cerro Grande (ESP)Assistant VAR: Jerome Brisard (FRA)
PREVIOUS MEETINGS

This will be the fifth meeting between Napoli and Arsenal, and the first since the 2018/19 Europa League quarter-finals. We have won three of the previous four (L1), keeping a clean sheet in all three victories.

We've ventured to Naples just once in the Champions League, back in December 2013 when we lost 2-0, with Mikel Arteta sent off during the match, but we still progressed to the round of 16, finishing second in the group, helped by a 2-0 success against Neapolitans in N5 when Mesut Ozil and Olivier Giroud were on target.

Our most recent visit brought more joy in the Europa League. Having won the quarter-final first leg 2-0 courtesy of an Aaron Ramsey strike and a Kalidou Koulibaly own goal, an early long-range free-kick from Alexandre Lacazette gave us an all-important away goal in Naples, and saw us progress to the last four.
LIVE COVERAGE

There will be live commentary of the game on Arsenal.com and The Arsenal app (download now on iOS/Android) from just before kick-off, when Dan Roebuck and Adrian Clarke will be behind the mics guiding you through all the on-field action.
You can also find out which broadcasters are showing the action live, wherever you are in the world.

items.titleEn: Arteta on Champions League return and Napoli trip
items.summaryEn: Ahead of our trip to Naples, Mikel Arteta has given his thoughts on the beginning of our Champions League campaign.
bodyEn: On the eve of our Champions League opener against Napoli, Mikel Arteta can't wait to get our European campaign underway as we aim to continue our trajectory in the competition.

In Mikel's first three campaigns as our boss in Europe's premier competition, we have progressed from quarter-finalists to semi-finalists, and last term finished as runners-up as we go deeper and deeper into the knockouts.

We begin our quest to make the final step in our quest for European glory away from home in Naples on Wednesday, and Mikel is relishing the challenge the Serie A side poses, and what this continental campaign might bring.

“I’m really excited,” our manager said. “We know what this competition means to all of us, the experience of last year as well, so we need to start with the first game in a really, really tough place, but really excited to start the campaign.
“Start well tomorrow; that's the only thing we can do. Start by putting in a big performance tomorrow to increase the probability of winning the game.”

The Neopolitans finished second in the Italian top-flight last term, and appointed six-time Scudetto winner Massimiliano Allegri as manager in the summer as they aim to also make one giant leap forward again in 2026/27.

They boast a formidable home reord in European competitions down the years, but we head to southern Italy with some excellent away form, having suffered just one defeat in the last 12 Champions League matches. So what does the boss put that down to?

“The consistency in the performances that we put in and the fact that we have been really dominant even when we play at home,” he said. “With our identity, with what we want to achieve in games, believing and being convinced that we can do it.

“It will be a really tough place, I've been in that stadium before, I know the atmosphere they create, their record at home is really, really strong. They have a very experienced manager, a lot of players that played in the league as well, so we know the challenge ahead. We are prepared and we're ready to go.”

items.titleEn: In-form Calafiori relishing Napoli test
items.summaryEn: The Italian defender has made a fantastic start to the season and can't wait to kick off our Champions League campaign back in his homeland
bodyEn: Riccardo Calafiori is looking forward to getting our Champions League campaign underway back in his homeland against Napoli
We travel to Naples to start our fourth straight campaign in the competition, aiming to go one step better than last season when we reached the final for the second time.

Our left-back has been one of our standout players so far, starting all four matches, scoring and providing two assists and relishing bringing the form that earned him a Premier League Player of the Month nomination into European action.

"I'm excited," Riccardo said. "It's also nice to start in Italy, in Naples, a special city, and I'm really looking forward to playing this game. I think it will be amazing, especially for a Champions League night, the stadium will be buzzing for sure and I can't wait to play.
"We started [the season] in a perfect way, I would say, and I hope we can keep going like that."

The perfect start Riccardo is referring to has seen us win four games from four, beating Manchester City in the Community Shield before securing Premier League victories over Coventry City, Aston Villa and Chelsea.
Our Italian defender has particularly enjoyed the way we've gone about winning the games, with his role as an attacking full-back proving enjoyable.

"I always enjoy a lot to play with my teammates, and the way that we're playing, especially in the beginning of the season, it's amazing," he added. "The flow that we have, I think you can see on the pitch, and I enjoy it a lot."
"I think the boss and the staff saw that I had this [ability], and they tried to help me as well with the timing of the movements and where to go.
"But of course, I'm a defender, so I also need to help the team in that sense. When I'm occupying this position, there's always another player who's try to help me or defend me."

Riccardo will be hoping to continue his flying start to the season in his home country as we travel to the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona for our first game of the league phase. We were as close as we've ever been to winning the competition last season, as we ultimately lost the final on penalties to Paris Saint-Germain.
But Riccardo, along with the rest of the squad, feel that we have the confidence and form to make a positive start to a run he hopes will lead to another final, this time in Madrid.
"I think you could see from the last two editions that we won most of our games and the first time we've been to the semi-final and last season we got to the final," he said.
"So it's really important for us and we have to keep going. We are really confident at the moment, especially with all these results that we achieved."

bodyEn: Arsenal’s preparations for their opening Champions League game against Napoli have been disrupted after they were caught up in the travel chaos that affected airports across the UK.

Mikel Arteta was forced to cancel his pre-match press conference at the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona on Tuesday after Arsenal’s flight was severely delayed by an air-traffic control issue. The Arsenal manager and his players are understood to have remained at the club’s training ground in Hertfordshire as they waited for the delay to pass after completing their morning session as usual.

Club sources have insisted there has been no alteration to their planned schedule other than arriving later than expected to the team hotel. Uefa has also agreed to allow Arsenal to cancel their mandatory press conference due to the delays, which have also affected supporters travelling to Italy for the match.

Jurriën Timber is set to be part of the Arsenal squad for the first time since the Champions League final defeat by Paris Saint-Germain on 30 May after recovering from a groin injury. The Netherlands defender missed the World Cup due to the problem that has dogged him since March but Arteta said before Sunday’s win over Chelsea that Timber was close to returning.
Cristhian Mosquera is still absent with a muscle issue but Marli Salmon, the 17-year-old defender who signed his first professional deal last month, is also part of the 23-man squad.

Arsenal won all eight of their group stage matches in the Champions League last season on their way to the final and have only lost one in their last 12 away games in the competition. But as they prepare for one of Europe’s most intimidating atmospheres, Arteta insisted they must take one game at a time despite starting the season with a 100% record in the Premier League.
“That puts us in a really good situation. The energy and the confidence around the team is high – now we have to show that,” he said.
“I’ve been in that stadium before, I know the atmosphere they create. The record at home is really, really strong. We know the challenge ahead. We are prepared and we’re ready to go.”

Napoli finished as runners up behind Inter in Serie A last season, but have made a poor start this season under their new manager, Massimiliano Allegri. Kevin De Bruyne is expected to feature against Arsenal but they are without Scott McTominay, who had a successful surgical procedure to treat an irregular heartbeat yesterday. The 29-year-old is expected to resume training in two weeks.

Napoli are also are likely to be without influential former Fulham midfielder André-Frank Zambo Anguissa as Allegri takes charge of his first Champions League match for four years. “People in this town have passion for the team, we have to start winning games again,” Allegri said. “We know we are challenging a very strong team – Arteta has done extraordinary things. Let’s face it with pride and desire.”

bodyEn: The concourses are silent when, deep in the Emirates Stadium’s bowels, Chief Inspector Pete Dearden’s briefing begins. Arsenal’s 4.30pm kick-off against Chelsea is still hours away but the fixture carries significance as a London derby and because the Premier League champions are hosting a realistic challenger.

Dearden is a senior officer in the Metropolitan police’s public order command and Sunday’s matchday commander. He is, to borrow football jargon, giving the pre-match team talk, running through intelligence and in-game tactics. “Set the right style and tone,” he says. After Dearden has finished, the police room becomes a pseudo-station for the afternoon, with all incidents triaged by the same crime officer. Football offences can be found in niche legislation, and the Met wants London’s matchdays to be, so far as possible, policed uniformly.

Matchday is the iceberg’s tip. The Met’s 17 dedicated football officers (DFOs) each work full-time on one club, planning each fixture with the matchday commander. All 500-plus games the Met covers per season are risk-graded using factors such as risk level of supporters, proximity, recent history and kick‑off time. Dearden labels Sunday’s game “medium medium”.

“Our mantra is safety, security and service,” Dearden says. “We appreciate that with 60,000 people in the stadium not everybody is going to behave, but we want to reduce the overall risk of the likelihood of disorder.”

Three police support units (PSUs), each containing an inspector, three sergeants and about 21 constables, have been assigned to the match. In addition, there are the senior team and 20 operational football officers, or “spotters”, on duty.

Clubs also have their own in-house safety teams, with, in effect, both parties doing their homework before collaborating. Arsenal’s operation involves about 1,000 stewards and response team members. They are the first responders to any incidents within Arsenal’s footprint. When a Chelsea fan overzealously reacts to his team’s early lead, the response team remove him.

Stadiums are not policed as standard, but clubs can request (and, if the request is accepted, pay for) special police services (SPS). Arsenal asked for one PSU to work within the Emirates for Chelsea’s visit but even then, police intervene only when required. Dearden estimates policing football costs the Met £23m a season, with approximately 10% recovered from clubs for SPS.

The Met is looking to close that gap, with aspects such as road closures and hostile vehicle mitigation now managed, and financed, by clubs. Dearden says his department is looking at “mitigation measures to reduce risk, which means that we don’t have to have as many police resources and we don’t compromise safety and security”.

Using spotters is one such measure. They work under the DFOs, are usually locally based for their day-to-day duties and operate consistently with one club. Dearden estimates that their expertise allows them to do the work of double the number of public order officers that would otherwise be needed. “They will go to pubs in the wider footprint where these people gather and try to identify what their plans are, get a good feeling for their mood and the numbers,” Dearden says.

Some Chelsea spotters are in Holborn and will follow when supporters journey to Arsenal by tube. Fans being unwilling to engage with spotters may indicate they are planning something. “You can get a good idea of whether they are potentially going to cause problems at a game because of that lack of engagement,” Dearden says. “It’s that communication approach again – even with some of the supporters that cause us problems, albeit a minority, there’s still engagement to be had. There are still opportunities to say: ‘Don’t do that.’”
Immediately before the match one spotter performed CPR on a supporter. The intervention was life-saving.

Outside the Emirates, two blue vans contain officers monitoring the data from cameras scanning passersby as part of an intelligence‑led live facial recognition pilot. The trials were funded thanks to a multimillion-pound Premier League investment.

Passing the cameras is voluntary, with signs alerting pedestrians to their presence. Faces are biometrically scanned and compared with a watchlist containing the several thousand people subject to football banning orders (FBOs) and individuals wanted for more serious crimes.

“We are targeting high-harm offenders, sex offenders, those with FBOs, who, if they came to an event, could spoil it for others, commit crimes, or exploit opportunities such as crowded spaces,” Dearden says.

The two-hour pilot yields six interventions, one while Guardian Sport is present. Officers intervene to speak to the individual, who is with their family. They have an FBO, although are not restricted from being around the Emirates. They have also recently been released from prison for human trafficking and are wearing a tag.
Dearden feels half a dozen hits is proportional to what would be expected. “What we can’t measure is the deterrent effect,” he says.

Noticeable is the relative lack of police visibility compared with recent years. That is by design, not accident. A heavy police presence does not necessarily make an event feel safe. “We don’t work on a ‘just in case’ basis these days,” Dearden says. “We deal with known knowns.” Arsenal fans in Naples on Wednesday are likely to meet a vastly different approach.

Immediately before the match, the Guardian laps the ground with the day’s three-person violence against women and girls (VAWG) team. “We want to change the culture of what perhaps in the past was tolerated,” Dearden says, giving the example of staff being targeted with misogynistic abuse.

“We’ve had people at football matches come forward and say: ‘I’ve heard you talk three or four times now and I’m now confident enough to report that I think I’m a victim of domestic abuse and controlling behaviour.’”
The VAWG team are also watching for those who may target vulnerable individuals.

For the match, Dearden heads to the command room with Arsenal’s safety team and the other emergency services. Proximity and open dialogue are vital. Because of the game’s risk level, there is a bronze commander, Inspector Rachel Duckett, at ground level. A half-time briefing allows all parties – including medical, the London fire brigade, the local authority, the Premier League, and British transport police – to compare notes and address issues. Dearden and Duckett then discuss the strategy for the game’s end.

For all the planning, much of what happens at football is result-driven. With Arsenal 2-1 up and time running out, a late Chelsea equaliser might have changed the mood. Home and away fans cross paths after, outside the 3,000-strong Chelsea end, where there is no cordon. Arsenal supporters gloat; some Chelsea fans react. A pair of Chelsea content creators try to record in the middle of the departing crowd and receive an expletive-laden reaction from passing Arsenal fans. They are advised to move on for their own safety.

Striking is the speed at which potential flashpoints are spotted and then defused. Officers are calm, not confrontational, and act as an external subconscious: “‘C’mon, think – do you really want to do that?’”

An hour after the final whistle, the stadium is silent again, and Dearden and his senior team debrief pitchside. A dozen incidents occurred around the game, with two arrests made – one for assaulting a steward and another for racial abuse and assault. A further 10 people were reported for offences including drinking in view of the pitch, missile throwing, low-level assault of a steward, homophobic chanting and possession of drugs.

Dearden says the number is “slightly higher than we’d like” but points out that it demonstrates proactivity. For example, stewards are told not to tolerate pushes as simply part of the job. Outcomes will be proportionate and consistency is key. In the days and weeks ahead, everything will be analysed, assessed, fed into data. Incremental improvement will be sought and further action may be required for the reported incidents.
But, for a few hours at least, all involved can reflect on a matchday’s work completed well.

bodyEn: There have been seasons when Chelsea have turned up at the Emirates Stadium and parked the bus. “You know, I think 10 years without a title is boring,” José Mourinho said in response to criticism from Arsenal fans after a stultifying 0-0 draw in April 2015. On Sunday, though, there was no holding back from Chelsea. “I want to compete in the best possible way to win,” Xabi Alonso said after seeing his new side edged out by Arsenal in a breathless encounter. “Today we didn’t want to sit deep from the first minute. We wanted to be active.”

The plan worked at times. Chelsea maintained their habit of scoring early goals, going ahead through Morgan Rogers, and created further openings. But they were facing the champions and do not have Arsenal’s completeness. Shortcomings were exploited, particularly in midfield. Declan Rice romped through the middle at one point and the winning goal owed much to Reece James losing track of Martin Ødegaard as Arsenal’s captain strode through to fire past Emiliano Martínez.

It was expected to be a key battleground, and the way Arsenal went 2-1 up was felt keenly by Chelsea given their difficulties on deadline day, when Enzo Fernández got his £125m move to Manchester City and no one was signed to replace the Argentinian. However, it is worth remembering Chelsea were short not only of Fernández’s offensive skills as they fell to their first defeat under Alonso. It was also significant that Moisés Caicedo was out again, an unspecified issue proving a nuisance, and it is a concern that Alonso lacks a suitable stand‑in for the Ecuador international whose ability to cover ground, snap into challenges and shield his defence would have come in handy against a midfield as powerful as Arsenal’s.

There is much to like about Alonso’s vision. Chelsea are not obsessed with possession and are speeding forward on the counterattack. Yet while they look menacing with every attack there is a cost to the chaos. Alonso has found balance elusive. Chelsea have conceded seven goals in three games, are without a clean sheet in the league since January and need the oomph provided by Caicedo if they are to make this full-throttle style work.

Caicedo, such an important presence since joining for £115m in 2023, is yet to start this season. He missed the 3-2 win against Fulham and was replaced 14 minutes after coming on during the 4-3 victory against Brighton. Alonso is erring on the side of caution. He stressed there was no long-term problem after the Arsenal game and admitted Caicedo was rushed back against Brighton. “I don’t want to make the same mistake again,” Alonso said, keeping the wider picture in mind. It is a long season, even with no European football, and the physical demands of the league means there is no point Caicedo playing through pain when doing so would surely cause more problems down the line.

As it stands, though, Chelsea are too open and cannot strengthen until January. Compromises are necessary but the jury is out on some fixes.Alonso is a believer in James, whose shift from right‑back to central midfielder started under Enzo Maresca, but the captain is learning the role and his lack of feel for the position was exposed by Ødegaard.

Arsenal found the gaps. Roméo Lavia started alongside James but is yet to complete 90 minutes since joining Chelsea three years ago. The Belgian has struggled with injuries and ran out of steam against Arsenal after an hour, at which point Alonso looked to his bench and replaced Lavia with Malo Gusto, leaving his expensively assembled side to play out the closing stages with two repurposed right-backs in the middle.

This was never the plan. Chelsea looked at replacements for Fernández. They wanted Alex Scott but Bournemouth would not sell. Crystal Palace’s Adam Wharton has admirers, there was interest in Roma’s Manu Koné, whilea move for Monaco’s Lamine Camara, which collapsed as the summer window closed, left Chelsea fuming.

In January Chelsea will hope to find a player more suited to Alonso’s system than Fernández, who is not the most mobile. They are not missing him in an attacking sense. Chelsea are scoring and the bigger headache is what to do out of possession. They do not have another player with Caicedo’s skillset.

Dário Essugo was billed as Caicedo’s deputy when he joined last year but does not have Alonso’s trust and has been loaned to Strasbourg. Jordan Henderson is recovering from a broken wrist and is 36, and sending on Gusto over Valentín Barco was an early pointer. Barco, signed from Strasbourg this summer, is promising but the 22-year-old is inexperienced and, in any case, is more passer than destroyer.

Arsenal started with Rice, Ødegaard and Myles Lewis‑Skelly in midfield. They kept the £75m Bruno Guimarães in reserve and brought on two Spanish World Cup winners in Mikel Merino and Martín Zubimendi, another player wanted by Chelsea.

The gulf in midfield resources told and it was the absence of Caicedo that mattered most for Chelsea. Perhaps Alonso could have adjusted and fallen back. If Chelsea continue to look so vulnerable at the back in the big games the tactics will be called naive. Yet Alonso will trust that sticking to his ideals will be rewarded in the long run. This is the start of a process. He is introducing a new system and accepts it comes with risks. The problem is that he does not have a midfielder to put out fires if Caicedo is out.

bodyEn: Three league games played, three games won. For Arsenal this season could only have started better if Manchester City, who look like being one of their two most serious challengers, had dropped points. But it’s not just about results: Arsenal have been comfortably the better side in each of those three games, approaching each of them in very different ways.

After the controlled victory over Coventry City and the tight game against Aston Villa that was won thanks to ratcheting up the pressure in the 15 minutes after half-time, came success in a far more open game in which they conceded for the first time this season. Chelsea tested Arsenal on Sunday, went ahead, and yet Mikel Arteta’s side still always looked like they would win – even if it did take a superb late save from David Raya to keep out an Estevão shot. But the goalkeeper too is part of their strength; even if an opposing team can work a shooting opportunity, Raya has the capacity for spectacular saves that can dispirit opponents.

Arsenal threatened from set-pieces but also from open play; they can beat opponents in multiple different ways, even when Declan Rice, probably their player of the season last year, has an off day (his unpunished late trip on Morgan Rogers was cynical and nasty, one of those deliberate offences miles from the ball that the game would benefit from treating as a red card offence).

The uplift may simply be confidence, the pressure of not having won the title, of those three successive second-place finishes, now lifted. But there are also individuals who look sharper, livelier, fresher than they did at any point last season. Martin Ødegaard is perhaps the most obvious. He struggled with injuries last season and scored only one goal; already this season he has two in the league and one in the Community Shield. Some players return from the World Cup and look exhausted or find the readaptation to the grind of the domestic game difficult; Ødegaard seems reinvigorated.

There is an imagination to his play, a lightness, and he took his goal against Chelsea superbly. His link-ups with Kai Havertz, another at times mercurial presence, were often delightful, conjuring space and angles where none seemed to exist and bringing the winner. In a team that last season developed a reputation for uncompromising physicality, there is something almost otherworldly about seeing two such ephemeral talents combining, sprites glimmering on a castle wall.

But it’s not just Ødegaard. For Bukayo Saka, last season felt like chickens coming home to roost. He is only 25 but Sunday brought what was already his 205th league start, while playing regularly for England as well. Fatigue had been stored up, which is always a worry for players who emerge as early as he did. Thomas Tuchel didn’t use him in the World Cup semi-final for reasons of tiredness or injury that remain opaque (the situation was promptly confused when he scored a hat-trick in the third-place game). But he seems back to something like his best in the early weeks of this season, fizzing in from the right-hand side and delivering dangerous corners on demand.

The other standout in the early weeks of the season is Riccardo Calafiori, who has already developed a very promising relationship going forward with Christos Tzolis, even if a few issues remain to be resolved defensively on that flank. The Italian, who scored Arsenal’s opener in the Community Shield, is not only a threat from set-plays but is very good at breaking through the lines, making him a real weapon against low blocks.

Chelsea are improving. Xabi Alonso’s side were far less open through midfield than they had been against Fulham and Brighton – easier as that can sometimes be to manage against sides who don’t instinctively cede possession. It may be, especially as the attrition of European fixtures strikes others later in the season, that they emerge as a very serious force. Arsenal, though, are very, very good now, and that means they could be several points clear by the time that putative Chelsea challenge emerges.

Arteta’s side are not merely playing with great authority; the fixtures have also fallen well for them, getting Villa away and Chelsea at home while both sides are still finding their patterns of play. It’s still very early. We haven’t even got to the first international break yet. Pitfalls are always waiting, and football is not a sport that reacts well to being taken for granted. But for Arsenal, their title defence could hardly have started better. Things could change but, at this moment, it seems more likely that they’ll have it won with several games still to play than that their grasp on the title will have slipped.

bodyEn: David Raya says Arsenal are playing with greater confidence after the “relief” of winning the Premier League. The champions continued their perfect start to the defence of their crown with the 2-1 home win against Chelsea on Sunday, making it nine points out of nine.

It was a powerhouse performance coloured by a freedom of expression, which stood in contrast to the nerviness of the final months of last season when the team laboured under a weight of pressure and expectation before they beat Manchester City to the title. That was Arsenal’s first triumph since 2004 and followed three consecutive runners-up finishes.

The shackles were off against Chelsea, just as they have been for much of the season, beginning with the 3-0 win against City in the Community Shield. Kai Havertz and Martin Ødegaard scored the goals against Chelsea and provided most of the creative flourishes. But it was the ferocity of the collective intensity, the sheer physicality, that took the breath. Raya pulled off a stunning late save to deny the Chelsea substitute Estêvão. Arsenal did not deserve to drop points. It was an ominous statement of intent.

“Winning the league after that many years and after those years that you are so close … it gives you that relief and it gives you that extra confidence,” Raya said. “Coming from the three games this season, especially the Community Shield, winning against City, the way we played against them – that gives you extra motivation and extra confidence to play the way we want to play …
“Hopefully we can keep playing this way because we know how good we are. We know we can beat anybody in this league. Let’s just focus on the moment and be in the present.”

The most eye-catching aspect of the display was how Arsenal reacted to going behind after 77 seconds to a Morgan Rogers volley. They attacked in waves and created a remarkable number of openings before Havertz equalised in the 25th minute. The belief could also be felt in the stands where there was no panic, only bellowed encouragement.

“There’s things to improve on that goal [by Rogers],” Raya said. “We had to defend a little bit better, especially right at the start of the game. It was disappointing to concede that goal. But the main thing is the reaction that we had after it and the way we played. The way we dominated, the way we attacked, we defended.
“We know how good Chelsea are, especially in transitions, and the way the play is dragged back to defend. So it was a really important win.”
